sections.heading: Admitting that I can do ministry without your life in it
sections.text: God, I have to admit that I can be busy doing your work while depending very little on you. I can speak, serve, lead, and pray with my mouth moving and my heart half-asleep. I can go through holy work in an unholy way—without love, without joy, without clear dependence on your help. Please forgive me for treating ministry as something I can manage on my own. Wake me up inside, and make my service alive with your presence.
theological_themes: Ministry can be outwardly active while inwardly lacking dependence on God.
True service requires God’s power, love, and spiritual life rather than mere human effort.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitful life and work come from abiding in him, and that apart from him his disciples can do nothing of lasting spiritual value. This directly grounds the confession that ministry without God’s help is empty.

Paul warns that impressive spiritual speech and sacrificial service can be worthless if love is absent. That supports the prayer’s concern over heartless service that may look religious but lack God-shaped love.

sections.heading: Confessing my hunger for approval
sections.text: I see something ugly in me: I often want people’s approval more than I want your pleasure. I let their opinions feel like the measure of whether I have done well. When something good has happened through me, I should give you the credit. When I have sinned, I should grieve and turn back to you. Instead, I keep checking how I am being seen. Lord, expose that in me and set me free from it.
theological_themes: The fear of human opinion can become a false rule for ministry.
God deserves glory for any good done through his servants, while sin should lead to mourning and repentance.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts seeking human approval with serving Christ, making clear that the desire to please people can corrupt faithful ministry. This speaks directly to the prayer’s confession of making others’ opinions the standard.

Paul refuses to make human judgment the final measure of his ministry and looks instead to the Lord’s evaluation. The passage supports the prayer’s desire to live before God rather than before public approval.

sections.heading: Owning the hidden motives in my preaching and praying
sections.text: Forgive me for the ways I can preach, pray, counsel, or stir others up spiritually while secretly wanting praise for myself. That is deceitful. I can call people toward you while wanting them to notice me. Teach me to see myself honestly before you—not to perform humility, but to know how much mercy I need. Keep me low enough to serve gladly and truthfully.
theological_themes: Religious speech and leadership can be mixed with self-seeking motives.
Humility requires honest self-knowledge before God, not a public performance of lowliness.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus warns against practicing righteousness in order to be seen and praised by others, including acts of prayer. This directly illuminates the danger of using spiritual activity to gain commendation.
Paul calls believers to reject selfish ambition and conceit, and to regard others with humility. That supports the prayer’s longing to be freed from ministry driven by self-importance.

sections.heading: Letting my weakness display your grace
sections.text: Thank you that my weakness does not make me useless to you. You often show your strength most clearly where I feel most inadequate. So help me not to hide every weakness as though your reputation depended on my competence. Help me admit my limitations without despair, and without making myself the center. Let people see more of your grace because I am obviously not enough on my own.
theological_themes: God displays his power through the weakness and frailty of his servants.
Honest acknowledgement of weakness can magnify God’s grace rather than disqualify faithful service.

scripture_references.connection: The Lord tells Paul that divine power is made perfect in weakness, leading Paul to boast in weaknesses for Christ’s sake. This is the central biblical foundation for rejoicing in infirmity without discouragement.

Paul describes gospel ministers as fragile vessels carrying a treasure so that the surpassing power is seen to belong to God. That closely matches the prayer’s desire for God’s glory to be clearer through human insufficiency.

sections.heading: Depending on power beyond my own
sections.text: Teach me to work by a strength that is not naturally mine. Call me into things I could not do without you, and help me endure burdens I could not carry without you. Let everything I do be for Christ, with Christ’s power carrying me. Make my ministry truly yours—not a project I own, not a platform I protect, but work that belongs to you from beginning to end.
theological_themes: Christian ministry requires supernatural enabling, not merely natural ability.
Serving Christ includes both attempting work beyond one’s strength and enduring hardship beyond one’s strength.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes his ministry as labor carried out with Christ’s energy powerfully working within him. This supports the prayer’s request to act by strength beyond natural capacity.
Paul says his sufficiency for ministry comes from God, not from himself. The passage grounds the prayer’s desire for a ministry that is truly God’s rather than self-produced.

sections.heading: Learning from Paul and leaning on you
sections.text: Lord, let me learn from Paul. He did not impress everyone by appearance or polish, and he knew real weakness. Yet you called him faithful and used him. Keep me from measuring usefulness by charisma, reputation, or public strength. Let me lean on you as he did. Make me faithful, and let the ministry you have entrusted to me be carried by your power, for your glory. Amen.
theological_themes: God values faithfulness over outward impressiveness.
A minister’s usefulness rests in God’s calling and power rather than personal presence or eloquence.

scripture_references.connection: Paul says he came in weakness and fear, not with impressive rhetoric, so that faith would rest on God’s power rather than human wisdom. This strongly supports the prayer’s reflection on Paul’s unimpressive outward ministry and God’s effective power.

Paul thanks Christ for strengthening him and appointing him to service because Christ judged him faithful. This supports the prayer’s desire to be counted faithful and to receive strength for ministry from the Lord.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language about considering oneself “more vile than any man” reflects a Puritan style of intense self-abasement. I rendered it as honest self-knowledge and awareness of one’s need for mercy, preserving the force of humility without encouraging comparison as a literal psychological exercise.

The prayer assumes a ministerial context and names sins especially common to public spiritual leadership, such as preaching or praying for praise. The modern version keeps that setting rather than generalizing it into any Christian service.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted the repeated concern about serving without God’s power as a confession of self-reliant ministry, not as a denial that God can use flawed service.

I connected the request for supernatural power with God’s strengthening presence and, by implication, the Spirit’s enabling, while avoiding adding extended pneumatological language not explicit in the original.
I treated the references to Paul’s weak presence and unimpressive speech as drawn from Paul’s own reflections in 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians, emphasizing faithfulness over public charisma.
